Smart Injection Molding Machine Monitoring and Control with Wireless in Mold Sensors
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Even in the state of the art injection molding machines, molds are not normally equipped with sensors to monitor the process. Currently available mold sensor systems are costly, cumbersome to maintain, limited in their capabilities and are used only in situations where the product liability costs are high. This project proposes developing a system to control the injection molding machines with in-mold sensors that use asynchronous WiFi for communication. The in-mold sensors will provide in-process data to the injection molding machine to control the process, keep maintenance cost down, provide traceability for parts during service, and keep track of mold life and cycle history.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Symbolic CAD for Tracking Student Design Evolution
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Mechanical designs are represented by solid model files in a CAD system.  Most mechanical designs are performed by engineers trained at universities. During the CAD learning process, solid models are created by students, and student creation of files occur in a step by step basis.  By capturing the evolution of these files, step by step, using human readable symbolic representation, the investigators believe important data about CAD based design evolution can be obtained to monitor design intention as well as fluency in solid modeling. This proposed study attempts to better understand design through the medium of CAD design evolution by developing symbolic representation of design evolution in a CAD system

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
TITLE: Developing a tunable 3D Printed Membrane for Desalination
ABSTRACT:
New desalination technology(tunable 3D printed membrane) is proposed by professors from the UTRGV engineering school. The pore size of three elastic filaments printed to form a triangular stack (i.e. membrane) is pressed to change the opening by vertical pressure. At the right pore size, desalination is possible by placing pressurized seawater at one side of the membrane and allowing only fresh water pass through. It is expected to be fast-paced research and has great potential to be developed into a marketable product thus realizing a research enterprise and increasing research opportunities for the UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: SAR/ISAR Simulation for a Three Dimensional Hybrid Material Target
A Study on Design and Production Method of Nanofluidic Channels for On-Chip Spectroscopy
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Narrative Project Description
Spectroscopy can be used to detect explosives efficiently through the absorption response of organic materials in the mid-infrared range. A mid-infrared spectrometer typically consists of a broadband thermal emitter and broadband detector, external optics, as well as a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR). All these components can be incorporated into a single chip, and this will provide the advantage or portability and low cost. Lin P. T. et al. (2014) have developed a mid-infrared spectrometer for on-chip chemical sensing using silicon/silicon dioxide wave guides. The on-chip device still requires a sufficient concentration of the chemical in order to detect it and separate the signature from the background noise. The goal of this research is to build microfluidic channels in the wave guides that can concentrate the airborne particles present in the air to a level that they are detectable by chip-based spectroscopy.  
1.	Design and simulation of nano-fluidic channel
Detection of airborne particles require a deliberate design of flow passages for gas sampling. The flow of the fluid medium and the movement of the particles in it must be simulated using a computer fluid dynamics program. Micro- and nanofluidic devices are designed more commonly for liquid flow or multiphase flow applications. Microchannels are often classified as channels with a characteristic length (e.g. hydraulic diameter) of 10-200 μm, whereas nanochannels have hydraulic diameters under 0.1 μm (Kandlikar and Grande, 2003). In liquids, molecular mean free path is in sub-nanometer scale and therefore liquid flows in microchannels are treated with conventional fluid models. However, for gas flows in microfluidic channels, traditional fluid models based on continuum mechanics theories do not apply. Because the mean free path of air molecules at atmospheric conditions is about 70 μm, no-slip boundary conditions for larger channel flow do not apply to microchannels. Partial vacuum conditions that can occur in gas sampling flow passages further increase the molecular mean free path. For nanofluidic channels, the mean free path for gas molecules is significantly larger than the channel diameter. This means nanochannels should only be use in large numbers and short lengths, in order to attain a meaningful flow sampling. 
For gas flows with large Knudsen numbers (Kn = λ/L), traditional finite-volume or finite-difference method solvers for Navier-Stokes equations cannot be used as they are based on a continuum hypothesis. An appropriate simulation tool is the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method (Bird, 1994), which has been used for vacuum applications such as high altitude space crafts and laser ablation process. DSMC has also been used for some MEMS simulations.
One of the existing DSMC software tools is dsmcFoam, which has been developed as a part of the open source CFD package OpenFoam by Scanlon et al. (2010). This tool can be applied to both 2D and 3D flows that can be either steady or unsteady. By conducting probabilistic simulations of a large number of particles and their interactions within the simulation domain, the flow phenomenon is captured as a statistical average. For demonstration, they used dsmcFoam to simulate rarefied gas flows (Kn ~ 0.01) as shown in the figure below.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ISRP: Multiphase Flow and Heat Transfer in Micro-Channels for High Power Cooling Applications
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project aims at obtaining initial data for developing a larger external grant proposal (NSF MRI) in acquiring instruments for microfabrication and high speed imaging for a laboratory research in multiphase flow and heat transfer in micro-channels. Due to the characteristic boiling instability in narrow passages, two-phase flow boiling of liquids has not achieved its true potential for high power heat transfer applications in electronics, automotive, aerospace, and defense industry. The objectives of this project are to (1) construct a multiphase flow loop for calorimetric testing and flow visualization, (2) fabricate and test new micro-channel designs that can overcome the instability problem, and (3) develop a theoretical model that can be used as a design tool for microfluidic devices.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Feasibility of Biofilters to Reduce Pollutant Emissions in Diesel Engines
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers
INTELLCONT.EDITORS: H.E. Romejin, A. Schafer. R. Thomas
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Every year, heavy-duty diesel trucks (HDDV), such as commercial border trucks, idle for long periods of time waiting at the ports of entry, POE, of the United States, emitting gases such as, carbon monoxides (CO), Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), and oxides of nitrogen (NOx).These last two are not listed within the six critical pollutants by the Environmental Protection Agency, but they serve as precursors of ozone (O3), a major pollutant which has detrimental effects on human health and the environment. Among one of the emergent control technologies in existence is biofiltration. The biofiltration process allows the removal of contaminants present in the stream of air via biochemical oxidation of organic compounds by microorganisms. In this research, a biofilter for these vehicles is designed and adopted from existing biofilters to test the removal efficiency in diesel engines. The prototype of this design will be evaluated in the capture of emissions. This paper compares existing technologies and evaluates the feasibility of using a biofilter using basic principles such as, design, cost, process, and effectiveness. Other studies have indicated a greater than 90% efficiency, but design and costs for vehicle designed biofilters are still challenges to be pursued.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: INDIRECT ANALYSIS OF INJECTION MOLDING USING FLOW SIMULATION
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
The plastic injection molding process is widely used and of great importance for the manufacturing process production of plastic parts in many applications such as automotive, sports, electronics and many more endless applications. Injection molding process has many advantages, such as short production cycles, can be performed with many different types of materials, provides excellent surface of products and facilitates the molding of complicated shapes. However, in order to achieve benefits of injection molding process, proper design of mold is very critical. Often flow simulation software such as Moldlfow are widely used to optimize product design and process conditions for injection molding process. However, injection molding defect such as flash is not predictable since most flow simulation software does not provide as an option. 
Even properly designed mold can develop flash. Flash is caused by aging of mold, changes of resin and/or process conditions. Even though flash may not a major defect, it requires flash removal process and scrap rate increases during removal of flash process. 
In this research, production mold from Steel Case was chosen as a case study and flash was estimated by monitoring pressure at the point of flash. A least pressure condition was found and proved through test molding of sample at the optimum condition. Flash was effectively eliminated. .

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Missing Energy Considerations in Industry Operational Improvements: Two Case Studies
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers
INTELLCONT.EDITORS: K. Barker, D. Berry, and C. Rainwater
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: According to the Department of Energy (DOE), optimizing the efficiency of manufacturing processes can result in significant energy and cost savings. Process efficiency can be achieved through the implementation of productivity improvements which often can translate into increased production capacity and larger profit margins. Although most companies try to generate productivity enhancements, there often exists a disconnection between such improvements and the associated energy expenses/savings resulting from them. Using the DOE’s Industrial Assessment Center database, and case studies of two companies in the manufacturing sector of South Texas, relevant missing energy considerations regarding Direct Productivity Enhancements are identified. Companies search for improvements in energy assessments, “energy treasure hunts” and consulting engagements, but miss properly quantifying the impact. The research question focuses on quantifying the impact of missed productivity enhancements. With tools such as lean engineering and decision support tools, the two case studies are used to compute the energy impact. A comparison was drawn between current energy recommendations savings and expected savings from applicable productivity enhancements. Future studies consist in a comparison between the expected savings from the productivity improvements and actual savings after applying the energy considerations, and, a review of limiting factors affecting the implementation of these improvements.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Gas-Assisted Powder Injection Molding: A Study About Residual Wall Thickness
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
The effects of processing variables on gas penetration depth and residual wall thickness (RWT) of gas-assisted injection molding (GAIM) parts were investigated for polypropylene (PP) and 316L stainless steel powder feedstock (SUS316). The processing variables were melt temperature, shot size, gas pressure, and gas delay time. By using a Taguchi L9 array, the results were compared with the previous work. Mold material was also investigated by molding with both aluminum and Stereolithography (SLA) mold inserts at varying temperatures. The most significant parameter affecting RWT was melt temperature for PP and gas delay time for SUS316. Additionally for SUS316, it was found that gas penetration depth and RWT were decreased with increasing mold temperature.

While both computer simulation and experimental validation were carried out, the results from simulations failed to consider the effect of thermal conductivity differences between SLA and Al cavities due to lack of a coupled analysis capability in its module.

PRESENT.NAME: APS March Meeting
PRESENT.TITLE: Static Mixer for Heat Transfer Enhancement for Mold Cooling Application
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Injection molding is the process by which a material is melted in a barrel and then it is injected through a nozzle in the mold cavity. When it cools down, the material solidifies into the shape of the cavity. Typical injection mold has cooling channels to maintain constant mold temperature during injection molding process. Even and constant temperature throughout the mold are very critical for a part quality and productivity. Conformal cooling improves the quality and productivity of injection molding process through the implementation of cooling channels that ``conform'' to the shape of the molded part. Recent years, the use of conformal cooling increases with advance of 3D printing technology such as Selective Laser Melting (SLM). Although it maximizes cooling, material and dimension limitations make SLM methods highly expensive. An alternative is the addition of static mixers in the molds with integrated cooling channels. A static mixer is a motionless mixing device that enhances heat transfer by producing improved flow mixing in the pipeline. In this study, the performance of the cooling channels will be evaluated with and without static mixers, by measuring temperature, pressure drop, and flow rate. The following question is addressed: Can a static mixer effectively enhance heat transfer for mold cooling application processes? This will provide insight on the development of design methods and guidelines that can be used to increase cooling efficiency at a lower cost.

PRESENT.NAME: APS March Meeting
PRESENT.TITLE: Surface geometry modification for effective water spreading
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Liquid spreading on solid surfaces depend on the kind of materials (liquid, solid, and vapor) and the interface geometries. Many applications involving liquid deposition by spraying and condensation require deliberate management of liquid spreading over the surfaces. In this work water spreading on solid surfaces with geometrical patterns are observed by experiments in an environmental chamber, which is controlled for temperature and humidity. Water will be deposited to the surfaces through spraying and condensation on a Peltier cooling stage. An optical microscope camera is utilized to observe static and dynamic liquid spreading behavior during the tests. Various test samples of different surface wettability and geometrical modifications are created by 3d printing technique. There are numerous studies that uses chemical coatings for wettability modification providing an effective solution. But these conventional techniques have limited long term reliability when the surface is exposed to environmental contamination which degrades the wetting behavior over time. By adding geometrical features less than a millimeter in the length scale, sustained ``highways'' are created on the surfaces, which provide an effective method for liquid drainage path with long term reliability. A successful implementation will lead to increased efficiency of applications such as dehumidifiers, heating and cooling systems in buildings and power plants.
